questions.question: What is the correct order of the core Terraform workflow?
options: plan → init → apply
init → plan → apply
apply → plan → init
init → apply → plan
questions.explanation: init prepares the directory (providers, backend), plan computes the change set, apply executes it. validate/fmt slot in between init and plan.

questions.question: What does `terraform plan` actually show?
options: A list of all resources in the cloud account
The diff between desired config, recorded state, and refreshed reality — what would be created/changed/destroyed
The cost estimate of the infrastructure
The provider changelog
questions.explanation: Plan reconciles three views: your HCL (desired), the state file (last known), and the refreshed real-world values — producing the add/change/destroy set that apply would execute.

questions.question: Why is the state file critical?
options: It caches provider binaries
It maps resource addresses in code to real resource IDs — without it Terraform doesn't know what it manages
It stores the Terraform CLI version
It is only used for outputs
questions.explanation: State is the binding between `aws_instance.web` and instance i-0abc123. Lose it and Terraform will plan to create everything again (duplicating live infra); corrupt it and applies become dangerous. Hence: remote, encrypted, locked, backed up.

questions.question: Two engineers run `terraform apply` on the same state at the same time. What prevents corruption?
options: Terraform queues them automatically over the network
State locking via the backend (e.g., DynamoDB with S3, or Terraform Cloud)
Git merge conflicts
Nothing — it always corrupts
questions.explanation: Locking backends acquire a lock before mutating state; the second apply fails fast with 'state locked' instead of interleaving writes. A plain local or lock-less remote state has no such protection.

questions.question: What's the difference between a `resource` and a `data` block?
options: data blocks are deprecated resources
resource creates/manages infrastructure; data only reads existing infrastructure
resource is for AWS, data for Azure
data blocks can't have filters
questions.explanation: Data sources query things Terraform doesn't manage (the latest AMI, an existing VPC) so you can reference them; resources are owned by this configuration and appear in plans as create/update/destroy.

questions.question: Plan shows `-/+ aws_db_instance.main (forces replacement)` on production. Best first move?
options: Apply — Terraform knows best
Stop; identify the attribute forcing replacement, consider state mv (if renamed), lifecycle rules, or a non-destructive path
Delete the state file and re-import
Run destroy first to be clean
questions.explanation: -/+ means destroy-then-create — for a database that's data loss. Plans must be read, not just approved. Renames need `terraform state mv` (or moved blocks); some attributes support in-place alternatives; `prevent_destroy` guards against exactly this.

questions.question: The terraform.tfstate file may contain secrets in plaintext and should never be committed to Git.
questions.explanation: True. State stores all resource attributes — DB passwords, keys — as returned by providers. Use an encrypted remote backend with restricted access, and add *.tfstate to .gitignore.

questions.question: `terraform apply` on unchanged code and unchanged infrastructure will still recreate all resources.
questions.explanation: False. Terraform is declarative and idempotent: if desired state matches actual state, the plan is 'No changes' and apply does nothing. Recreation happens only when a diff forces it.

questions.question: During an incident someone hand-edited a security group in the AWS console. How does that surface in Terraform, and what's the disciplined fix?
options: It never surfaces; console changes are invisible
Next plan shows drift; either apply to revert to code, or codify the change in HCL and apply
Terraform blocks all future applies
Run terraform init -upgrade
questions.explanation: Plan refreshes reality and diffs it against code — the manual edit appears as a pending change. The team decides: revert (apply as-is) or adopt (update HCL first). Either way, code stays the source of truth.

questions.question: You must bring an existing, hand-created S3 bucket under Terraform management without recreating it. What's the mechanism?
options: Just write the resource block; Terraform auto-detects it
Write the matching resource block, then terraform import (or an import block) to bind it into state
Delete the bucket and let Terraform recreate it
Copy the bucket definition from the AWS console export
questions.explanation: Import writes the real resource's ID into state under your resource address; from then on plans manage it. Without import, Terraform would try to CREATE a duplicate (and fail on the unique name).

questions.question: Write the command to create an execution plan and save it to a file named tfplan.
questions.explanation: -out saves the exact computed plan; `terraform apply tfplan` then executes precisely what was reviewed — the pattern CI/CD pipelines use so nothing changes between review and apply.

questions.question: Write the command to list every resource tracked in the current state.
questions.explanation: `terraform state list` prints all resource addresses in state; pair with `terraform state show <addr>` to inspect one resource's recorded attributes.

questions.question: What is a Terraform module?
options: A provider plugin binary
A reusable, versionable package of Terraform configuration called with input variables
A single .tf file
A workspace
questions.explanation: A module is a directory of configuration with inputs and outputs, consumable via source+version. Organizations publish standard modules (VPC, service, database) so every team builds on the same paved road.

questions.question: What does `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` do?
options: Hides the resource from plans
Makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail with an error
Prevents manual console deletion
Skips the resource during refresh
questions.explanation: It's a guard rail inside Terraform: a plan/apply that includes destroying that resource errors out. It can't stop console deletion — it stops the far more likely accident of a careless terraform apply/destroy.

questions.question: Pinning provider versions (e.g., `version = "~> 5.0"`) is recommended so runs are reproducible.
questions.explanation: True. Unpinned providers can introduce breaking behavior between runs. Version constraints plus the .terraform.lock.hcl file make every machine and CI runner resolve identical provider builds.
